en.general: The minimal, species-typical genetic endowment for social cognition and learning that a human infant is born with -- attention to faces, voices, and others' emotions/actions from birth; discrimination of helpful vs. unhelpful agents by ~3 months; joint attention and shared symbol-construction by ~9 months; perceiving others' needs and a nascent fairness sense by year two; a temporally-extended, narrative sense of self by year four; internalization of social norms from age five. The 'kit' framing emphasizes that these are starting capacities elaborated through a social/cultural environment, not a finished cognitive architecture -- development of the full range of human social abilities (empathy, cooperation, language, norm-following) depends on growing up embedded in that environment, not on the genetic kit alone (see OE-PROPOSITION-culture-capacity-is-evolved-nature).

examples: A 9-month-old pointing to share attention on an object with a caregiver, before having any language to name it.

Six-year-olds spontaneously establishing shared rules to fairly divide a limited resource without adult instruction -- built on the starter kit's early fairness sense, elaborated through social experience.
